text: Picture a company with fifty separate databases sitting on the exact same logical SQL server — one per client, say. Without parameters, connecting to all fifty means building fifty nearly identical linked services, each one differing only in a single database name. Parameterizing solves this directly: define that value as a parameter instead of a fixed one, and pass in the actual value at run time.

While editing a linked service, look for the Add dynamic content link sitting underneath any configurable field, like the database name box. Any field that can actually accept a parameter shows this link — genuinely easy to miss the very first time you're looking for it.

Selecting it opens the Add dynamic content panel, where you can write an expression directly, or select the plus button to create a brand-new parameter right there on the spot — reusable the moment it exists.

Underneath all of this, a parameterized linked service's JSON gains a parameters block, and the value that used to be fixed becomes a live expression instead. Whatever actually calls this linked service supplies the real value at run time — the linked service itself never changes, only what gets passed into it does.

One firm rule worth remembering for good: never parameterize a password or a secret directly. Store every real secret in Azure Key Vault instead, and parameterize only the secret's name. That closes out Chapter 2. Next, Chapter 3 finally puts everything you've connected to actual work: pipelines and activities.
